newsitem.title: USA: Chevrolet portrays new minivan as freedom machine.
newsitem.headline: Chevrolet portrays new minivan as freedom machine.

text.p: In selling its new Chevrolet Venture minivan to the public, General Motors Corp. will try to tug on buyers' heartstrings and portray the vehicle as a freedom machine.

That image is usually reserved for sexy, top-down roadsters or brawny sport/utility vehicles, but Chevrolet officials believe their new ad campaign breaking this week can secure a bigger beachhead in the crowded and brutally competitive minivan market.
The campaign, which features the tag line "Let's Go!" is estimated to be worth about $50 million, according to industry trade publication Advertising Age.

The Venture and similar vans from Pontiac and Oldsmobile, which are now arriving in dealerships, replace GM's plastic-bodied APV minivans, which were much maligned for their long snouts and awkward driving positions.

The new vans feature a much more conventional design and are aimed at the same "soccer mom" and family hauling market that has made Chrysler Corp. the dominant minivan maker, with more than 45 percent of U.S. minivan sales.
The GM minivans, along with several new sedans that are being introduced this year, are critical to GM's quest to regain lost market share and boost profitability.

Chrysler, which invented the minivan in 1983, pioneered new features in 1995, such as dual-side sliding doors -- which are now being copied on the Venture and other vans coming from Toyota Motor Corp. and Honda Motor Co. Ltd.
Karen Francis, the brand manager for the new Venture, said minivan advertising up to now has been focused mostly on features and function, and very little on emotion.
"We'd like to show that owning a minivan can be a fun, good, great thing," she said.
The "Let's Go!" tries to suggest that the minivan is so functional that it can allow families to get more things done, have more adventures and have a better quality of life, Francis said.
"It's our 'Just do it'," she said, referring to the popular Nike athletic apparel campaign.
Part of the campaign includes sponsorship of a 22-city shopping mall tour for Walt Disney Co.'s "Hercules" animated feature film, which premieres in June.

One of the campaign's television commercials features a 1960s hippie couple in a flower-plastered van. As times change, they "morph" into a '90s family, while their vehicle morphs into a Chevy venture.
In another, computer-generated dolphins jump through the rear doors of the van to show that it has the widest opening doors on the market.

And a third, highlighting van's separate front and rear sound systems, shows a toddler tossing her toys at the control panel to tune to an opera station. Much to the amazement of her parents, she sings along with the opera in Italian -- a feat accomplished by computerized special effects.
Chevrolet's Venture starts at $20,495, including destination charges, the Pontiac Trans Sport starts at $21,619, while the Oldsmobile Silhouette starts at $22,245.
Chevrolet expects to sell about 80,000 Venture minivans in 1997. In 1996, Chrysler sold 538,807 minivans, while Ford sold 209,033 Windstar minivans.
